national.title: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro heading for Ecuador, Argentina says
national.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential election, was en route to Ecuador after stopping off in Argentina with his family, an Argentine agency said. Earlier, a State Department official told CBS News they would receive U.S. visas.
national.body: Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family were en route to Ecuador after leaving Brazil and stopping off in Argentina, the Argentine National Directorate of Migration said on social media. Bolsonaro lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend.Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters arrived in Argentina Tuesday night through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing, the directorate said, then boarded a private plane for a flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador.Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami's Opa Locka executive airport, The Associated Press reports. It wasn't clear whether Bolsonaro and his family were on board.Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, and his family will be allowed entry into the U.S., the official said. Bolsonaro departed Brazil for the U.S. after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, according to multiple Brazilian media reports.A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. His campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment. Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil."A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."Mr. Trump told reporters early Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., though he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina."I

national.body: A senior Iranian official denied Wednesday that Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal, saying instead that Qatar had come with "unacceptable" ideas, the Reuters news agency reported. national.title: Four investigations Democrats could launch if they win Congress
national.summary: Democrats have promised a wave of probes into the Trump administration if they win back the House.
national.body:
Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections.

While their success is by no means guaranteed, control of either chamber would give the party power to issue subpoenas, as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year.

Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November.

Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations.

"We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC.

Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities - particularly cryptocurrency firms - as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family.

national.summary: Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, and early voting is underway throughout the country.
national.body: Control of the House of Representatives will come down to a number of battleground seats. CBS News has identified 47 House districts that will likely determine which party will have the majority. Of those seats, 20 are currently held by Democrats and 27 are held by Republicans. Republicans currently hold a razor-thin majority, with 218 seats, plus an independent who normally caucuses with them. Democrats hold 214 seats. There are two vacancies. CBS News' Battleground Tracker model estimated on Sunday that Democrats are on track to take control of the House with 229 seats. There is still a path for the GOP to keep the House: The Battleground Tracker's estimates ranged from 215 Democratic seats — which would give Republicans a narrow majority — to 237 seats.

national.summary: The two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without reliance on Arab parties.
national.body:
With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted, with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.

His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.

A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.

In Israel's fragmented political system, the signs are that Netanyahu's main rival, the former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, would struggle to command a parliamentary majority without parties led by Israel's Arab minority. According to partial results, they have equalled or gained on their previous record number of seats.

On the campaign trail, most Jewish opposition parties pledged not to work with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values.

national.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
national.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".
national.body:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

national.body: The U.S. military said it attacked a boat it accused of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Tuesday, killing five people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America. The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed by the U.S. military's boat strikes to at least 240 in more than 70 strikes. The Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025. As with most of the military's statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes and that "intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narcotrafficking." But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing "narcoterrorists." Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the U.S. over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India. The attacks have drawn intense scrutiny from some Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars. The Pentagon's watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the U.S. military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the lethal operations, which include a military commander's intent, target development and execution. national.title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
national.summary: Student voters studying outside their hometown have a right to choose where they register to vote. Advocates say a Montana legal fight is a reminder of a misunderstanding of those students' rights.
national.body:
Students at the University of Virginia help eligible voters register to vote in Charlottesville, Va., in 2024. Ryan M. Kelly/AP hide caption

Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?

A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.

That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day .

Only on NPR Advocates worry new bans on student IDs will trip up younger voters Now, as the wait continues for the judge's final ruling, some experts on student voting see the case as a reminder of common misunderstandings about the rights of some of the country's youngest voters.

Voting in the U.S. is tied to residency, and state and local governments determine who qualifies as a resident who can register.

To make sure certain voters, such as eligible students, are not discriminated against, federal law sets ground rules for residency requirements, explains Michael Hanmer, a professor of government and politics at the University of Maryland, whose research has focused on student voters .

"You can't apply different standards to different groups of people, so college students need to be treated the same as anybody else in the mix here who might be new to a particular place," Hanmer says.

national.title: Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds
national.summary: The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.
national.body:
The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.

The group analyzed the federal ICE program, called 287(g), that deputizes state and local police for immigration enforcement. It used the agency's public records and information requested by the Deportation Data Project, which is based at UC Berkeley and UCLA and collects U.S. immigration enforcement data.

More than 29,000 officers were deputized by ICE between January 2025 and October 2026. That's far more than the 11,600 deportation officers directly employed by ICE.

Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at FWRD, says her organization's analysis highlights just how big a role these partnerships have played in the Trump administration's immigration enforcement work. The program was created in the 1990s under the Clinton administration but was little used — until President Trump returned to office.

"These state and local officers are a key lever in the administration's quieter approach to enforcement . They're trading what used to be splashy urban surges, which we saw in Chicago and Minneapolis , for just routine highway stops now under the 287(g) program," Rose told NPR ahead of the report's release.

The most common and most aggressive form of these 287(g) partnerships, the Task Force Model, allows police and sheriff's departments to make immigration arrests. And, in return, as long as these local agencies remain in "active and ongoing participation in 287(g) enforcement activity outlined" in the agreements signed with ICE , they get money to spend on new cars, equipment and other enforcement resources.

The Department of Homeland Security has said that 287(g) is a critical tool to cut down on crime and illegal immigration.

Law enforcement agencies in Florida and Texas, combined, accounted for about half of the more than 47,000 immigration arrests made nationally between January 2025 and August 2026 through 287(g), FWRD found.

national.title: Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations
national.summary: In several competitive U.S. Senate contests, candidates have built healthy campaign accounts with out-of-state donations. But the messages to those donors is very different from the one back at home.
national.body:
In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.

Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

The funneling of funds has affected at least four of the competitive Senate races, where a majority of the money is coming from outside the state. ActBlue and WinRed, two major grassroots fundraising platforms, are a major catalyst for out-of-state fundraising.

Because this technology is inexpensive to run, it incentivizes candidates to rely on digital ads, according to Zachary Albert, a professor of politics at Brandeis University.

"ActBlue and WinRed really reduced the transaction costs for contributing," Albert said. "Even if you're only yielding like a $5 or $10 contribution from someone like the costs of soliciting that are so much lower than they used to be, that it makes it worthwhile."

With both parties — and each candidate — now having fundraising platforms, political hopefuls increasingly need to stand out from the crowd and are often shifting their messaging to a broader audience, which can result in using polarizing messaging to solicit funds.

For in-state and out-of-state ads, candidates tend to have two different sets of talking points, according to Wesleyan Media Project's Michael Franz.

Only on NPR Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many "In a general election campaign for a [local] TV ad, a candidate will never say, 'I'm the Democrat,' because they want to appeal to moderates and swing voters and they want voters across the aisle," Franz said. "But with a digital ad that's airing outside of your state, the party label becomes more important."

national.title: Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations
national.summary: In several competitive U.S. Senate contests, candidates have built healthy campaign accounts with out-of-state donations. But the messages to those donors is very different from the one back at home.
national.body:
In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.

Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

The funneling of funds has affected at least four of the competitive Senate races, where a majority of the money is coming from outside the state. ActBlue and WinRed, two major grassroots fundraising platforms, are a major catalyst for out-of-state fundraising.

Because this technology is inexpensive to run, it incentivizes candidates to rely on digital ads, according to Zachary Albert, a professor of politics at Brandeis University.

"ActBlue and WinRed really reduced the transaction costs for contributing," Albert said. "Even if you're only yielding like a $5 or $10 contribution from someone like the costs of soliciting that are so much lower than they used to be, that it makes it worthwhile."

With both parties — and each candidate — now having fundraising platforms, political hopefuls increasingly need to stand out from the crowd and are often shifting their messaging to a broader audience, which can result in using polarizing messaging to solicit funds.

For in-state and out-of-state ads, candidates tend to have two different sets of talking points, according to Wesleyan Media Project's Michael Franz.

Only on NPR Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many "In a general election campaign for a [local] TV ad, a candidate will never say, 'I'm the Democrat,' because they want to appeal to moderates and swing voters and they want voters across the aisle," Franz said. "But with a digital ad that's airing outside of your state, the party label becomes more important."

Sources had told the BBC earlier on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had arrived in the US.

In a tweet , external , the migration authorities said that he, his wife and two daughters had boarded a private flight headed towards the city of Guayaquil in Ecuador shortly after crossing the border.

It is not clear whether Ecuador would be his final destination.

Earlier on Tuesday, a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country, were they to request them.

When reporters asked US President Donald Trump about Bolsonaro and his family's whereabouts later, he said: "I heard he was in Argentina."

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts started hours after Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations.

national.title: Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling
national.summary: President Donald Trump said that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.
national.body:
President Donald Trump throws a hat into the crowd as he arrives at a campaign rally at Lubbock Memorial Civic Center, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas. Annie Rice/AP hide caption

BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil. That's equivalent to about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.

Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.

Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.

The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is released into the atmosphere or burned off as a waste product by oil drillers.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency's "Super Emitter Program" that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.

national.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
national.summary: The King is on a nine-day tour that will take him to three countries, including the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda.
national.body:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

national.summary: Israelis voted in a national election set to shape the country's next government, with the Iran war looming large over their decisions.
national.body:
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, October 28, here . See earlier developments below.

The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.

Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.

According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.

Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.

While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.

One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

national.title: Iran war has cost $47 billion, U.S. military says
national.summary: The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.
national.body: The war with Iran has cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.The bulk of the war's price tag is the cost of replacing expended munitions, which CENTCOM pegged at around $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. The military also tallied $6.1 billion to replace lost equipment and around $11.9 billion in incremental costs like support for American service members.The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which were targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.By comparison, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers three months ago the war had cost around $37.5 billion, not including damaged U.S. bases.The Congressional Budget Office said last month the war could cost $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues, in part due to the need to replace interceptor missiles to defend against Iranian attacks. That cost could rise during tit-for-tat exchanges between the U.S. and Iran, which were common over the summer but have been quiet in recent weeks. CBS News has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.The Iran war will enter its ninth month this week, and the conflict's future is unclear. President Trump has suggested he might restart hostilities with Iran after next month's midterm elections unless Iran agrees to a deal. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," he told supporters during a rally in Florida last week.The Pentagon's inspector general said last month the U.S. is facing "strategic inventory shortfalls" due to the number of munitions expended during the war, leading the Defense Department to work to speed up production. The Trump administration has argued the military isn't facing shortages, with Mr. Trump saying in early September, "we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use."The administration asked Congress to approve tens of billions of dollars in supplemental military funding earlier this year, in part due to the Iran war. That request has not yet passed, and Democrats have pressed Hegseth for a more detailed accounting of the war's cost.

national.title: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science
national.summary: AI has made some awesome scientific discoveries. But now, questions are being raised about its accuracy
national.body:
A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.

His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.

Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.

Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous Navier–Stokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.

But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.

They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".

OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".

It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.

local.title: Local couple brings semipro basketball back to Rochester
local.summary: Chaniah Martino and Howard Jeffries are the owners of The Rochester Reapers Organizations, a men's semiprofessional basketball team.
local.body:
Rochester is once again home to a semiprofessional men's basketball team. The Rochester Reapers became part of the American Basketball Association league earlier this year.

The owners, Chaniah Martino and Howard Jeffries, are a young couple who found a way to fuse both of their passions to create this new organization.

"Once I realized that basketball was something he loved and business was something I loved, I figured we might as well put it together," said Martino.

The former caterer brought the idea to her fiancé, with three team name options. They both agreed that "Reapers" was most suitable.

"They're on demon time," Martino said to describe her players, using a slang term for a state of rigor and tenacity. "They're not coming to play."

The team's roster consists of veteran and rookie ABA players who have established comradery on and off the court. Jeffries said he intentionally drafted a group of men who he believes are "out for the same mission."

"The guys that I've picked are guys that I know want to work together," Jeffries said. "They're going to do anything it takes to get the win."

The Reapers are not Rochester's first professional or semi-pro team. The Rochester Seagrams formed in 1923 but in 1945, when they joined a forerunner to the NBA, they became the Rochester Royals. The team moved to Cincinnati in 1957 and exists today as the NBA's Sacramento Kings.

local.title: Attorney general needs to stick to law
local.summary: Saritha Komatireddy isn’t a household name for many New Yorkers. And that’s too bad, because she could be your next state Attorney General. We know all too well what we will get statewide by electing Letitia James as attorney general – more lawsuits that are so tinged by party politics that it’s har
local.body:
Saritha Komatireddy isn't a household name for many New Yorkers. And that's too bad, because she could be your next state Attorney General.

We know all too well what we will get statewide by electing Letitia James as attorney general – more lawsuits that are so tinged by party politics that it's hard to discern whether or not the case makes sense. That happens, in part, because James has been smacked down by courts often enough in her attempts to fill her prior campaign pledges to make life hard on President Donald Trump that it's hard to tell where a case actually exists or if James is just pandering to her supporters.

In our view, that shouldn't be a question when it comes to the state's attorney. Let’s not forget the First Department Appellate Division throwing out a $464 million liability verdict against Trump and the Trump Organization in August 2025 that was ruled to violate the Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Earlier this year James led a multi-state coalition of 19 attorneys general suing the Trump administration over executive orders giving Elon Musk’s DOGE access to federal payment systems that was dismissed by a federal judge.

James is also fond of saying the Attorney General’s office doesn’t have a hand in local criminal cases while backing Democratic Party-backed policies like bail reform, Raise the Age, decriminalization of minor offenses, cashless bail, discovery reform and others.

Komatireddy, on the other hand, has said during her campaign that she will try to chart a bipartisan path forward to fix New York’s bail system, including pushing reform that allows judges to consider someone’s dangerousness when considering bail. She would also use her office to help local prosecutors by sending attorneys to help with manpower and prosecutions.

The most striking difference between James and Komatireddy, however, is a willingness not to abandon fairness for political points. We have seen time and again that James is an attorney general who doesn't hide her opinions, whether those opinions are in regard to President Donald Trump or the Cornell University fraternity rape allegations. We need an attorney general who keeps their opinions to themselves and lets the law be their guide. As a federal prosecutor in the Eastern District of New York, Komatireddy has prosecuted high-profile cases involving international terrorism, cybercrime, narcotics trafficking, money laundering, fraud, and foreign public corruption while arguing before federal courts, leading national security investigations and advising on matters of foreign affairs, criminal law, and cyber policy.

local.body:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. (AP) -- If the Baltimore Ravens play like they did in the second half against Cincinnati, not even Lamar Jackson can save them.

Already facing a reputation for folding late in games, the Ravens were a caricature of themselves Sunday, outscored 35-0 in the final two quarters of a 35-13 loss to the Bengals. Jackson missed a third straight game with an ankle injury, Baltimore didn’t take full advantage of its statistical domination in the first half and then Cincinnati scored touchdowns on its first five possessions of the second.

The Ravens have outscored opponents by 65 points in the first half this season, while being outscored by 70 in the second. First-year coach Jesse Minter suggested the issue is at least partly psychological -- Baltimore isn’t handling momentum swings very well. He also indicated Monday that the team could use more leadership from players.

“There’s moments in the game where it’s like, ‘Who’s the guy that’s going to grab everybody together and get them together on the sideline?’ As a team we’re working through who that is,” Minter said. “There’s guys that want to do it, and there’s guys that, maybe they’re dealing with something, or they’re not playing the way they want to play, so they don’t feel like they can do it in those moments.

“If you’re kind of a known leader, sometimes you have to even erase how you’re playing if you feel like you can collectively get everybody out of a funk,” he added. “Those are things I think we’re just continuing to work towards, but yeah, I think there’s moments where we need a little bit more.”

The Ravens are 4-3, which isn’t itself cause for panic, but that record also has Baltimore in last place in the AFC North. Now the Ravens have to play at Buffalo this weekend, then have a quick turnaround before a Thursday night home game against Jacksonville.

“I think he’ll be in a decent spot, but we’ll know a lot more on Wednesday,” Minter said.

The first half. More specifically, the Ravens -- even with Tyler Huntley at quarterback -- have started well in games offensively, with offensive coordinator Declan Doyle using receiver Zay Flowers impressively.

local.body:
FALCONER -- A near full moon hung above the soccer pitch at Falconer High School Wednesday night as Jamestown Community College (JCC) earned a spot in the Region 3 women’s soccer championship game with a 2-1 victory over Herkimer College.

The opening minutes mirrored the final score, as both teams found space and tested the opposing goalkeeper in a back-and-forth battle.

In the 18th minute, sophomore Kaylyn Carnes put her boot to the ball, but Herkimer’s goalkeeper was up to the task, keeping the game knotted at 0-0.

The Generals had opportunities to net the game’s first goal in the 27th and 42nd minutes, but sophomore Angel Busch came up big, making two of her four saves on the night.

JCC had another chance to take the lead in the 37th minute, but Avery Johnson sent her shot just wide of the net, and the teams went into halftime scoreless.

That scoreless deadlock continued into the 83rd minute, when the intensity reached another level and the Jayhawks responded in front of a packed house filled with green and gold.

First, Kennady Ellsworth settled a ball in the box and tapped it over to Alexandria Halstrom, who buried the attempt to give JCC a 1-0 advantage.

The capacity crowd had barely finished celebrating when freshman Gracie Chimera finished an assist from sophomore Kaylyn Carnes. In less than a minute, Jamestown had built a 2-0 lead, sending Jayhawk Nation into a frenzy in the stands.

A poetry reading by guest writer Natalie Scenters-Zapico will be hosted by the State University of New York at Fredonia on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The event is at 7 p.m. in the Marion Art Gallery at Michael C. Rockefeller Arts Center is free, and the public is invited to attend.

Scenters-Zapico is the author of three collections of poetry, "My Perfect Cognate," "Lima :: Limón" and "The Verging Cities." In addition, she is the winner of the PEN/America Joyce Osterweil Award, the GLCA New Writer’s Award and the Utah Book Award. Her books have been reviewed widely in publications and broadcasts including The New Yorker, National Public Radio, The Washington Post and Publisher’s Weekly.

Scenters-Zapico's latest poems have been published or are forthcoming in publications such as The Paris Review, The New Republic, Yale Review, Kenyon Review, Colorado Review, New England Review, Best American Poetry 2024 and more.

Today, Scenters-Zapico teaches in the undergraduate and MFA creative writing programs at the University of South Florida, where she won a 2022 Faculty Outstanding Research Achievement Award and a 2023-2024 McKnight Junior Faculty Fellowship. She is also the Inaugural Director of the Michael Kuperman Memorial Poetry Library at USF.

local.summary: The village of Fredonia water system appears in deep trouble again. It was hit with a boil order Tuesday, days after a conservation order. Fredonia had to buy 966,000 gallons of water from the city of Dunkirk over the weekend, Mayor Michael Ferguson said Monday at a regularly scheduled Board of Trus
local.body:
The village of Fredonia water system appears in deep trouble again. It was hit with a boil order Tuesday, days after a conservation order.

Fredonia had to buy 966,000 gallons of water from the city of Dunkirk over the weekend, Mayor Michael Ferguson said Monday at a regularly scheduled Board of Trustees meeting.

The boil order was announced by the village Office of Emergency Management at 8:45 a.m. Tuesday morning. The stated reason for the order was "High turbidity levels and treatment deficiencies."

Fredonia water customers should bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute, then let it cool before using for: drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice, food preparation and washing produce, and preparing baby formula.

Officials will conduct "Water sampling after levels stabilize. The order will remain in place until testing confirms the water is safe," the Office of Emergency Management order stated.

The boil order is likely tied in with the conservation order, which officials say was spurred by recent dry weather which taxes the filters at the reservoir.

Ferguson said at the Monday evening village Board of Trustees meeting that Dunkirk transferred 966,000 gallons of water to Fredonia over the weekend, through a pump station on Vineyard Drive.

Ferguson said the flow from Dunkirk was shut off Monday morning. He acknowledged, "The draw for water is more than we can produce right now. Hopefully that changes shortly."

local.body:
A bagpiper in a kilt led hundreds of Azusa Pacific University students and the school president into the Cougars’ stadium before kickoff against Whittier College earlier this season, a sun-splashed celebration of what once were two of the biggest brands in California small-college football.

Azusa Pacific had dropped the sport in 2020 after 55 years and Whittier in 2022 after 115 years, mainly for financial reasons.

The two are back on the field, not in a full reembrace of the sport’s tradition and what it can do to enhance campus culture, but for another reason: Administrators saw an opportunity to bump shrinking enrollment numbers, a problem shadowing hundreds of colleges and universities across the country. Football rosters, after all, can number about 100 players and the sport is seen as a popular marketing anchor.

The two schools are among 10 four-year colleges and universities that started or restarted programs this season, the most in a single year since 2013, according to the National Football Foundation. Seven schools have announced plans to start programs in 2027 or later.

Azusa Pacific won the 1998 NAIA Division I championship and became a full NCAA Division II member in 2013. The Cougars made playoff appearances in 2016 and ’18, but a decline in the number of West Coast Division II football schools made travel too costly.

School president Adam Morris said he first approached athletic director Gary Pine about restarting football five years ago. A $1 million private gift funded startup costs, and the school moved from Division II to Division III and joined a Southern California-based conference. APU will begin competition in women’s flag football in the spring.

“Yes, it’s an opportunity to grow enrollment and there is some financial upside to the decision,” Morris said. “Really, it’s a great opportunity to touch the lives of 110 young men who will leave this place to go out into this community and have an impact in a significant way.”

APU’s on-campus fall enrollment is 1,900, down 46% from 3,359 in fall 2020. APU brought in 652 freshmen (49 were on the football roster) and transfer students to campus this fall, up 19% from a year ago. The school’s online learning program raises total enrollment to about 6,000.

local.title: Prevention best protection against cancer
local.summary: October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to recognize the importance of early detection, regular screening and improving women’s health. local.body:
October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to recognize the importance of early detection, regular screening and improving women's health. It is also an opportunity to talk about prevention and the steps we can take to reduce the risk of cancer.

Smoking remains the leading cause of preventable disease and death. In New York State, 9.9% of adults smoke cigarettes and 6.3% use e-cigarettes. And for women, smoking has been marketed to us as glamorous, stylish, fierce, and trendy... even a way to control weight. However, tobacco use contributes to cancer and negatively impacts every organ in our body. Women who smoke for more than 10 years appear to have approximately 10% higher risk of developing breast cancer compared to/with women who have never smoked.

Breast Cancer Awareness Month reminds us that screening can save lives, and prevention and healthy lifestyle choices matter too. Helping women -- and all New Yorkers -- break free from smoking and nicotine-use should be part of routine health care. Furthermore, smoking-related health care costs New York an estimated $12.07 billion each year.

Through Health Systems for a Tobacco-Free WNY, we work with health care and behavioral health organizations to strengthen tobacco screening, treatment and cessation support. Our goal is to ensure that every patient who uses tobacco is offered evidence-based support to quit. Learn more at: Health Systems for a Tobacco-Free NY (HSTFNY)

For New Yorkers who are ready to make a quit attempt, the NYS Quitline provides free and confidential support. This October, the Quitline is also promoting its Quit to Win Pet Campaign, giving New Yorkers another reason to take that important first step toward quitting. Find more information at: Quit for Your Pet! – NY Smoke Free.

Let's remember that protecting women's health goes beyond screening. We can ensure people have the tools and knowledge they need to live long, happy, healthy lives.

Amanda Hucksoll is an employee at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center.

local.title: State vows to continue funding free school meals
local.summary: Governor Kathy Hochul announced New York state will continue to fully fund its universal free school meals program despite President Donald Trump’s nationwide cuts to federal food assistance programs. By ensuring New York’s program remains fully funded, Hochul is protecting approximately 2.5 million
local.body:
Governor Kathy Hochul announced New York state will continue to fully fund its universal free school meals program despite President Donald Trump's nationwide cuts to federal food assistance programs. By ensuring New York's program remains fully funded, Hochul is protecting approximately 2.5 million free school meals per school day for kids across the state - and helping their families save up to $1,600 per child per year on groceries.

This past week, new reports revealed other states across the nation are now facing declines in free school meal participation due to the impacts of federal cuts and changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that are leading to Americans, including families with children, losing SNAP as a result of the Republican-led HR 1 bill that was passed last year and enacted by President Trump. However, those troubling impacts will not prevent New York schools from accessing the funds needed to continue providing free school meals. By continuing to fully fund the universal meals program that she launched last year, Governor Hochul is protecting millions of kids and their families from losing access to the free school meals they rely on.

"It's shameful that President Trump and Washington Republicans are trying to take free school meals away from our kids - and that's why I took action to ensure kids across New York won't lose access to the free school meals they rely on," Hochul said.

New York's universal free school meals program was enacted by Hochul last year and ensures that 2.7 million students across the state have access to free school breakfast and lunch. That law requires all school districts, charter schools and nonpublic schools that participate in the national school lunch and breakfast program to provide free breakfast and lunch meals to all students regardless of their families' income.

This year, Hochul fought for and secured a $395 million statewide investment in universal free school meals as part of New York State's FY27 Enacted Budget - representing an increase of $55 million above the previous fiscal year. Due to this increased State funding and Governor Hochul's commitment to continue fully funding the program, the federal government's cuts to food assistance will not result in any New York schools receiving less funding for free meals - ensuring that no New York student would lose access.

With approximately 2.5 million free meals served per school day, State officials estimate that schools across New York have already served approximately 75 million free school meals since the current school year started in September. Free school meals are estimated to help families save up to $1,600 per child per year on grocery costs.

local.body: Many know Dr. Ebony Prohet Bullock as the interim superintendent of Buffalo Public Schools, a leader focused on supporting educators, students and families. local.title: City garbage truck strikes and kills man in a wheelchair
local.summary: Capt. Greg Bello said officers responded to Hudson Avenue and Warsaw Street around 3:30 p.m. for the report of a pedestrian struck and found the man dead at the scene.
local.body:
A man in a wheelchair was struck and killed by a Rochester garbage truck Tuesday afternoon, city police said.

Capt. Greg Bello said officers responded to Hudson Avenue and Warsaw Street around 3:30 p.m. for the report of a pedestrian struck and found the man dead at the scene.

Police said the garbage truck was traveling east on Warsaw Street and trying to make a left turn onto Hudson Avenue. The man was operating his motorized wheelchair northbound in the shoulder of Hudson Avenue when the truck hit him, police said.

In a statement, Mayor Malik Evans shared his "deepest condolences to the family and friends" of the man who died.

"Members of my City team are committed to conducting a thorough investigation to determine how this accident happened and what can be done to prevent further tragedies like this one," Evans said. "We will share updates as the investigation progresses."

The truck driver, a man in his 50s, was not injured. Police said it doesn't appear that drugs or alcohol were a factor.

The incident remains under investigation and anyone with information, including video, is encouraged to call 911.

local.title: Niagara neighborhood calls for permanent relocation from radiological testing
local.summary: After state and federal radiological testing found dangerous conditions near Gill Creek in the Town of Niagara, neighbors are asking for permanent relocation, not just temporary housing.
local.body: After state and federal radiological testing found dangerous conditions near Gill Creek in the Town of Niagara, neighbors are asking for permanent relocation, not just temporary housing.It has been a long year for Lexi Hawk. She’s received letters from the State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), seen employees at her house sample soil and received test results that led the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to temporarily relocate her family.Just three blocks away from Lexi’s house, one of her neighbors, John Johnson, also got his test results back, and the radioactivity levels were so high that his family too was relocated.However, a few dozen people are living in the areas in and around their two homes that were never moved out during the testing or as remediation draws near."I want to get them to safety too," Hawk said. "I will always question what is beneath my feet. I will never feel safe there."The group founded by Hawk, Save Our Backyards WNY, is not asking for more of the temporary housing she and the Johnsons received. Instead, they’d like the government to fund a permanent relocation for the whole neighborhood."Call on the state and federal government to work together to establish a permanent relocation or a voluntary buyout program for affected families," Executive Director, Center for Health, Environment & Justice Jackie Medcalf said. "That means providing fair compensation so that homeowners can move into a comparable home.""If our two families didn’t step up, it didn’t seem like anybody was going to speak up," Johnson said.Johnson and Hawk said that it’s not just about protecting their neighbors, but their own families too, even after what Hawk believes will be full remediation work in the Spring."I know that I’ll be out of that house for another six months," Hawk said. "I’m just dreading the day that they call and say ‘it’s done and you have to go back,’ cause we’re not going back."WATCH: Niagara neighborhood calls for permanent relocation from radiological testing"How do you ever trust that this is really cleaned up? local.title: 'Truly sorry': Buffalo man sentenced to 5 years for Old Pink arson
local.summary: The Buffalo man who admitted setting the fire that destroyed the Old Pink in Allentown was sentenced to five years in federal prison.
local.body: The Buffalo man who admitted setting the fire that destroyed the Old Pink in Allentown was sentenced to five years in federal prison.John Burns, 42, was sentenced Tuesday by U.S. District Court Judge Richard Arcara after pleading guilty in July to arson of a building used in interstate commerce.The fire destroyed the Old Pink at 223 Allen St. on June 17, 2024.Burns had been kicked out of the bar after getting into a fight and later returned with a blowtorch, setting a fire at the back of the building. The longtime Buffalo institution burned to the ground.Burns was arrested less than three months later and initially allowed to go to a rehabilitation facility.But in May of last year, he was remanded after allegedly removing an ankle monitor he was required to wear while awaiting trial.Burns had faced up to 20 years in prison.During Tuesday's sentencing, Burns appeared in an orange jumpsuit with his hands shackled in front of him. His parents and several other family members were in the courtroom to support him.Arcara said he had received 23 letters of support for Burns that discussed his struggles with mental health, substance abuse and alcohol.WATCH: 'Truly sorry': Buffalo man sentenced to 5 years for Old Pink arsonThe judge also received a handwritten letter from Burns just hours before the sentencing hearing.In the letter, Burns apologized for the fire."I would like to express my deepest apologies to the community of Buffalo for setting the fire that destroyed the Pink," Burns wrote, adding that he was "truly sorry."Arcara noted that the fire could have been catastrophic, but no one was injured.The judge sentenced Burns to 60 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release. Burns was also ordered to pay $708,519 in restitution.

local.title: Bills rookies give local students special tour of the new Highmark Stadium
local.summary: A group of local middle school students got a special look inside the new Highmark Stadium Tuesday, with some of the Buffalo Bills' newest players serving as their guides.
local.body: A group of local middle school students got a special look inside the new Highmark Stadium Tuesday, with some of the Buffalo Bills' newest players serving as their guides.Dozens of students from Franklin and Hoover middle schools joined the visit, touring the Bills' new home and connecting with members of the Highmark Rookie Club."We were here with the children today, giving them stadium tours and just interacting with them," Bills rookie cornerback Davison Igbinoson said.The rookies spent part of their day off answering questions, talking with students and giving young Bills fans a chance to meet players they are used to seeing on television.For Igbinoson, the visit also offered an opportunity to show students that he was in their shoes not that long ago."I'm sure it's a big inspiration just being close to NFL football players, people that they only see on TV," Igbinoson said. "So I just want to talk to them and interact with them and show them that, like, I'm not much different than them. Ten years ago I was in middle school. I was having the same dreams and aspirations just as themselves."For many of the students, Tuesday marked their first time inside the new Highmark Stadium.WATCH: Bills rookies give local students special tour of the new Highmark StadiumSeventh-grader Avery Nicosia was among them."I was really excited, and I got to see all the rookies," Nicosia said.While meeting the players was a highlight, Nicosia said one part of the new stadium stood out in particular: the Bills' locker room."The locker room was, like, really cool," Nicosia said, pointing to the lights and video screens among the features that caught her attention.Igbinoson said the excitement from the students made the experience just as meaningful for the players."The reception has been great from the kids," he said. "I mean, the kids are big Buffalo Bills fans, and they love us, and we love them, so we just appreciate having them and their support."

entertainment.body:
The 2026 Toruń Camerimage Film Festival has unveiled its official program, bringing together some of this year’s top Hollywood and international awards contenders.

The 34th edition of the festival, which awards the Golden Frog for outstanding cinematography, runs Nov. 7-14 in Toruń, Poland. The main competition comprises 15 films, selected for the contribution their visual storytelling makes to the cinematic experience.

Among the high-profile contenders are Project Hail Mary , directed by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller and shot by Greig Fraser; Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day , with cinematography by Janusz Kamiński; and Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , shot by Ben Davis. entertainment.title: Academy CEO Bill Kramer Makes the Case for a More Global Oscars at Tokyo Film Festival
entertainment.summary: Kramer says international membership growth, the Oscars-YouTube deal, and a new festival-qualifying pathway to nomination are all part of the organization’s expanding worldwide ambitions.
entertainment.body:
The U.S. may be growing ever more isolationist under the “America First” rubric of President Donald Trump, but the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences remains steadfastly global in its outlook and ambitions.

That was the thrust of Academy CEO Bill Kramer ’s comments at the Tokyo International Film Festival on Wednesday, where he spoke at length about his organization’s ongoing efforts to bring more international filmmakers and film lovers into the Oscars fold.

“The Academy is becoming more and more global across programs, and as part of that, you’re seeing a great increase in the number of academy members who live outside of the United States,” Kramer said. He noted the oft-cited fact that a decade ago just 5 percent of Academy members were based outside the U.S., compared with 25 percent today. And in a hat tip to the local crowd, Kramer said the Academy has about 70 Japanese members, but that he expects that number to climb. Related Stories Movies Tokyo: 'All of A Sudden' Star Tao Okamoto Honored With The Hollywood Reporter's Trailblazer Award Movies Meet the Estonian Folklore Characters Helping to Celebrate the 30th Tallinn Fest - and Their Animator

“This is all part of our drive to create a more diverse and inclusive academy,” he said.

Kramer also underscored that Oscars nominations have already begun to reflect the increasingly cosmopolitan tastes of the member base.

“At the last Oscars, every category had international representation. It’s not just found in the international feature film category — this trend includes our best picture category,” he explained. “Of course, everybody remembers the moment when Parasite won best picture. That was sort of a pivot, or a shift, I think, in our thinking about what was possible with global cinema at the Oscars, and that continues.”

Kramer asserted that the Academy’s somewhat controversial deal with YouTube was inspired by this same desire to cultivate deeper ties with filmmakers and film lovers across the globe. The agreement gives YouTube exclusive global rights to the Oscars from 2029 through 2033, making the ceremony available live and free worldwide after ABC’s final telecast in 2028.

“In two years, the Oscars will be available on YouTube for free to 2.5 billion people around the world in over 30 languages,” he explained. “So, for the first time, everyone around the world will have access to the show at the same time and in the same format — and that is a huge, intentional move by the Academy to reach a bigger global audience.”

entertainment.title: Tokyo: ‘All of A Sudden’ Star Tao Okamoto Honored With The Hollywood Reporter’s Trailblazer Award
entertainment.summary: At a glitzy event at the Tokyo American Club, Hollywood and Japanese powerbrokers celebrated longtime industry and cultural links between the two countries.
entertainment.body:
All eyes were on Japanese actress Tao Okamoto as she received The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Trailblazer Award at a glitzy black tie gala event in the cavernous ballroom of the Tokyo American Club on Tuesday night.

The 2026 edition of American Film Night, a collaboration between THR Japan and the Motion Picture Association , took place during the Tokyo International Film Festival and saw top executives from the Japanese film industry, senior government ministers and leading local filmmakers and actors mingle with visiting Hollywood powerbrokers. Related Stories Movies Meet the Estonian Folklore Characters Helping to Celebrate the 30th Tallinn Fest - and Their Animator Movies Tokyo Film Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu Wants More Money, More Parties and a Bigger Global Profile for Japanese Cinema

The evening kicked off with a special message from Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi who extolled the cultural and political relationship between Japan and the U.S. — a running theme throughout the night with many references to America’s 250th anniversary.

“The close partnership between Japan and the United States in the film and media industry not only supports cultural exchange between our two countries. It is also a major driving force of the global entertainment economy,” said Takaichi. “Believing in the power of film and media to move the future, I hope this event will deepen exchange and partnership between Japan and the United States, and make it stronger still.”

In a nod to Okamoto, Takaichi added, “I extend my warmest congratulations to Ms Tao Okamoto, who receives the Trailblazer Award for opening new paths around the world with her brilliant talent and passion. The courage of pioneers like Ms Okamoto gives great hope to the next generation of creators.”

Okamoto, the model turned actress who starred in The Wolverine , Hannibal and The Man in the High Castle , and who this year was awarded the Cannes Film Festival award for best actress for her captivating performance in Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s acclaimed film All of a Sudden , was the center of attention on Tuesday night. Dressed in an elegant black dress, she received her award from MPA APAC president and managing director Urmila Venugopalan and THR Japan Chairman Tsukasa Shiga.

“My acting career began with the Hollywood film The Wolverine, released in 2013. Until then, I had been working as a model in New York. I had never imagined becoming an actor, so it was a big, unexpected gift,” said Okamoto in her acceptance speech.

entertainment.title: ABBA’s Mamma Mia! The Party Is Coming to Australia
entertainment.summary: The immerse, all-ABBA dining experience is booked for its Australian premiere in March 2027 at Sydney Event Centre at The Star.
entertainment.body:
Australians will have a chance to experience the full ABBA smorgasbord when the Mamma Mia party comes to Sydney next year .

Created by ABBA’s Björn Ulvaeus, Mamma Mia! The Party is an immersive theatrical dining event, where guests soak up the pop legends’ music in a restaurant recreated to look like a taverna on the Greek island of Skopelos, where most of the feature film was shot. Dinners are treated to Mediterranean cuisine and, of course, many of ABBA’s hits, performed by a live band and cast of 20 musicians and performers.

As the evening ends, fans can live out their “Dancing Queen” dream as the room becomes a 1970s-style disco. Related Foo Fighters Deliver a Blast From the Past on 'Kimmel': Watch Watch NE-YO Perform National Anthem at Game 4 of 2026 World Series in Tampa Bay Demi Lovato Offers Update After Allergic Reaction & Reported Hospitalization Explore ABBA See latest videos, charts and news

Mamma Mia! The Party is booked for its Australian premiere in March 2027 at Sydney Event Centre at The Star. It’s executive produced by Ulvaeus and Pophouse Entertainment, and TEG Dainty in Australia, whose president and CEO Paul Dainty was behind the Swedish group’s legendary tour down under a half century ago.

“Bringing Mamma Mia! The Party to Australia feels particularly special for me,” Dainty remarks. “I had the extraordinary privilege of promoting ABBA’s first and only Australian tour back in 1977, and I still remember the phenomenal excitement that followed them across the country.”

Through the friendships made on that first and only ABBA trek to these parts, ABBA’s Benny Andersson and Ulvaeus entrusted Dainty to tour Mamma Mia! 25 years later. The British-born concerts veteran also has the option to produce the hugely-popular ABBA: Voyage in these parts.

“Australia’s love affair with ABBA has never really ended,” Dainty adds, “their music has become part of our cultural fabric.”

He’s not wrong. Australia held the torch for ABBA when music tastes shifted, briefly abandoned, then came roaring back to Björn, Benny, Agnetha and Frida. The Melbourne-originated tribute brand Bjorn Again has been giving ABBA fans their fix since the late ‘80s and, in the ‘90s, the Aussie indie film Muriel’s Wedding introduced a new generation to the supergroup’s catalog.

entertainment.title: BMG Signs Australia’s Parcels to Global Publishing Deal
entertainment.summary: The independent music company will represent the Australian five-piece on a worldwide basis.
entertainment.body:
BERLIN, Germany — Parcels is the latest addition to BMG’s music publishing roster.

The independent music company will represent the Australian five-piece on a global basis, after signing a deal at the company’s European headquarters in Berlin.

Formed 2014 in Byron Bay, the picturesque beach spot on the most easterly point of Australia, Parcels relocated to the German capital in the mid-2010s, where they set about building their audience and shaping their sound.

It proved to be the right move. Daft Punk co-produced their 2017 single “Overnight,” which blew up and opened the gates for an international following, and festival spots everywhere from Coachella to Glastonbury. Parcels have accumulated more than 1.5 billion total career streams across three studio albums and several live efforts. Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

Through the new partnership, announced today (Oct. 28), BMG’s global network will “support Parcels’ international ambitions,” a statement reads.

The publishing agreement was led by Jasper Niebuhr, managing director, BMG Germany / Switzerland / Austria, in close collaboration with the company’s publishing teams across continental Europe, the United Kingdom, North America, and Australia, with key contributions from Alistair Norbury, Monti Olson, and Heath Johns.

“Parcels are one of the most distinctive and compelling bands of their generation,” comments Niebuhr in a statement. “Their extraordinary musicianship, songwriting, and creative vision have enabled them to build a truly global career on their own terms, without compromising what makes them unique.”

With their “Australian roots, creative history in Berlin, and strong presence in the U.S., they embody a truly international spirit,” Niebuhr continues. “We share their ambition to keep pushing boundaries and are excited to bring the strength of our global network to the next chapter of their remarkable journey.”

entertainment.title: Zara Larsson Smashes Venue Record at NZ’s Spark Arena
entertainment.summary: The Swedish pop star's sold-out Midnight Sun Tour of Australia and New Zealand wrapped with an historic two-night stand at Auckland’s Spark Arena.
entertainment.body:
The Swedish pop star has just completed her sold-out Midnight Sun Tour of Australia and New Zealand, which wrapped with an historic two-night stand at Auckland’s Spark Arena.

Larsson welcomed 12,796 fans to her first show on Sunday, Oct. 25, busting Spark Arena’s all-time record, according to Live Nation, which promoted the tour and operates the venue.

The following night, Oct. 26, she raised the bar again with 12,798 attendees. That’s 25,594 fans across the two nights, another record for the country’s biggest arena, which opened its doors to the public in 2007. Related Kenny MacPherson, Veteran Music Publisher and Big Deal Music Co-Founder, Dies at 71 Jessica Lynch

“Zara’s meteoric rise is unparalleled and a reflection of her talent, her warmth, and the genuine connection she has with fans around the world,” comments Mike Ross, tour promoter, Live Nation. “Breaking the all-time record at Spark Arena is a rarefied achievement amongst the many legendary names who have played the venue over the last 19 years – to do it twice, on consecutive nights, is incredible.”

Linkin Park previously held the record with 12,736 tickets sold for a show in March 2026.

“We are thrilled that Zara has broken the house record,” adds Mark Gosling, GM, Spark Arena. “It’s great to see artists pushing the boundaries of what’s possible at the arena, and Zara has set a figure that may be hard to beat. Congratulations to Zara and her team from all of us at Spark Arena.”

Earlier, on Friday, Oct. 23, she performed the biggest headline show of her career to almost 18,000 fans at Afterpay Arena in Sydney.

For her debut headline tour of Australia and New Zealand, Larsson swept in with 10 shows across six cities, all of them sold out.

entertainment.body:
The numbers are in: The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards was a No. 1 hit.

Presented Thursday, Oct. 22, the annual celebration of Latin music enjoyed a “strong multiplatform performance,” broadcaster Telemundo reports, to rank No. 1 in Spanish-language television for the 7pm-11pm primetime spot.

The broadcaster averaged 335,000 adults (18-49) and 1.1 million total viewers, according to data provided by Nielsen, peaking at 8:30pm with 400,000 adults (18-49) and 1.2 million total viewers. Related Foo Fighters Deliver a Blast From the Past on 'Kimmel': Watch Lars Brandle

At the same time, Telemundo’s digital platforms and social channels captured 306 million total views, up 57% from the 2025 edition, with fans watching a combined 29.7 million minutes, a 41% gain against 2025.

The 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards also powered “significant social engagement,” according to Talkwalker Social Content Ratings, for a No. 1 ranking across all TV in total social video views and the leading broadcast program of the day, regardless of language. Facebook, TikTok and Instagram led the way, while on YouTube, viewing minutes more than doubled (+101% vs. 2025), fueled by expanded livestream coverage.

With eight awards, plus the Billboard Vanguard Award, Fuerza Regida was the big winner at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Awards . Although not present, Bad Bunny was close behind with seven trophies, while Karol G, Peso Pluma and Romeo Santos won four each. Rosalía, Tito Double P and Prince Royce each took home three.

The ceremony aired live on Telemundo and Peacock from James L. Knight Center in Miami, FL, and featured 47 categories spanning major Latin music genres such as pop, tropical, Latin rhythm and regional Mexican. Additionally, for the first time fans had a historic opportunity to choose one of the night’s winners through a new award, Fan Favorite Artist, which went to Karol G.

entertainment.title: Hollywood Power Players (Like Bela Bajaria and Richard Weitz) Toast Honorees David Nevins and Peter Friedlander at Milestone Saban Clinic Gala
entertainment.summary: Alex Edelman, Walton Goggins and Connie Britton livened up the A-list fundraiser, which featured powerful speeches from the night's honorees and an impromptu round of applause for Bajaria.
entertainment.body:
Hollywood power players turned out in full force at Saban Community Clinic’s milestone 50th anniversary gala on Monday evening to toast a few of their own inside the Beverly Hills Hotel’s Crystal Ballroom.

The event raised a whopping $2.2 million for Saban — a network with seven clinics across Los Angeles (and a new 12,000-sq.ft outpost on the way in the Crenshaw corridor) that provide quality healthcare to anyone who walks through the doors — and it did so by packing the ballroom with A-list studio and network executives, agency partners, producers, actors and show creators like Dan Fogelman, Sam Levinson and Jonathan Nolan. Related Stories TV With 'Phony,' Nick Paley Poses a Horrifying Question -- But Makes It Funny TV 'Phony' Review: Connie Britton and Sam Nivola Lead Hulu's Likably Quirky and Beguiling Paranoid Mystery Series

A majority came to support the cause (growing more urgent by the day ) and celebrate the night’s headliner honorees, Amazon MGM Studios’ Peter Friedlander and former Showtime chief David Nevins , while others, however, quipped they couldn’t escape the gravitational pull of event linchpin Ellen Hoberman or longtime Saban champions like event chair Richard Weitz . The WME co-chairman was also responsible for one of the night’s heartwarming moments as he led an impromptu and thunderous round of applause for ousted Netflix chief content officer Bela Bajaria , his fellow event chair, during shared time at the podium at top of the show.

Weitz first congratulated Friedlander and Nevins for their awards before turning attention to Bajaria, “someone who has tirelessly worked for the industry, been a part of the clinic, and honestly somebody who has changed, I think, the face of Netflix — that’s my friend Bela,” he said. Weitz noted that his comments were not on the teleprompter but he wanted to take a moment to “give it up for her” because “she deserves the love.” Bajaria was ousted and replaced by Peter Rice in a major Netflix shakeup that saw her exit the streamer amid mass layoffs of 1,000 staffers. Weitz also acknowledged that he and Bajaria were Saban honorees together a few years back, “so it’s only fitting that we’re doing this together.”

It wasn’t the only nod to industry tumult from the podium but more on that — and Bajaria’s response to the ballroom love in her first interview since exiting Netflix — later. The current political landscape also played into the night’s festivities. Also at the top of the program, Hoberman noted how President Donald Trump and his administration have rolled back healthcare policies and cut programs like Medicaid, making it harder for vulnerable populations to get care. “If you want change, please vote,” said Hoberman, a philanthropist and longtime Saban advocate who is married to prominent entertainment attorney Tom Hoberman. “We must vote for leaders who will protect healthcare.”
